..(Tuesday through Sunday)
Issued at 419 PM EDT SUN OCT 11 2026

The extended period unfolds Tuesday through next Saturday,
shifting eastern Kentucky from unseasonably warm weather early
in the week to a sharp early-autumn freeze potential by next
weekend.

On Tuesday, a strong subtropical ridge will remain anchored
across the Southeastern US and Gulf Coast, keeping 500 mb
geopotential heights above the 99th climatological percentile
over the Deep South and between the 85th and 97th percentiles
over eastern Kentucky. At the surface, broad high pressure
positioned off the Atlantic Coast will maintain steady
south-southwesterly return flow across eastern Kentucky. This
pattern will yield warm, dry, and summer-like conditions for
mid-October. Afternoon highs on Tuesday and Wednesday will
climb into the lower to upper 80s, roughly 10 to 15 degrees
above seasonal normals. Tuesday and Wednesday forecast high
temperatures of 81 and 82 at the JKL airport are within 2 to 3
degrees of the established record highs of 84, set back in
1985. In fact, the 00Z LREF ensemble shows a 20 percent chance
of reaching 84 degrees on Tuesday and a 50 to 60 percent
chance on Wednesday. Model soundings Tuesday and Wednesday show
steep low-level lapse rates from the surface to 850 mb, with a
pronounced dry layer above the boundary layer. To account for
this boundary layer mixing, raw model guidance was blended with
the NBM to slightly lower dew points both afternoons.

Farther west, an upper-level trough ejecting from the Rockies
into the Northern Plains will push an initial, slow-moving
surface cold front into the Ohio Valley late Wednesday. Cloud
cover should gradually increase Wednesday afternoon from the
northwest, with rain shower chances slowly ramping up late
Wednesday afternoon into Thursday morning.

Some model spread remains regarding Thursday and beyond, driven 
by ensemble differences in the strength of the Southeast ridge and
the timing of the ejecting Plains shortwave. The initial cold 
front entering the Ohio Valley late Wednesday is shown by a
majority of models to stall and briefly lift back north as a warm
front on Thursday ahead of an approaching surface wave. However
some solutions are slower. NBM-1D viewer at the Jackson airport
has a 10-degree spread in high temperature guidance (69 to 80F), 
though ensemble consensus favors highs reaching the mid to upper 
70s. Isolated to scattered showers are forecast through Thursday 
night.

The secondary cold front sweeps across eastern Kentucky Friday
morning. Showers and storms will be scattered to numerous in the
morning, accompanying the frontal passage. Despite the early
precipitation, pre-frontal warming might still allow daytime
highs to reach the low to mid 70s ahead of the boundary.
Showers will shift southeast toward the Virginia, West
Virginia, and Tennessee state lines during the afternoon as the
front clears the area. Winds could be breezy at times, with
gusts likely up to 20 to 25 mph. The probability of the area
seeing gusts up to 30 mph currently ranges from a 40 to 50
percent chance in the latest 00Z LREF ensemble guidance. Strong
post-frontal cold air advection (CAA) will surge into the
Commonwealth late Friday afternoon and evening. Showers should
diminish Friday night as low-level moisture grows increasingly
shallow and temperatures drop into the upper 30s and lower
40s.

While there remains a great deal of uncertainty between
individual deterministic models (mainly the ECMWF and GFS),
ensemble cluster guidance shows overall good agreement on a deep
troughing pattern on Saturday. While GEFS-heavy clusters hold
onto cold northwest flow and low-level post-frontal clouds
slightly longer into the afternoon, dominant EPS/CMC clusters
favor faster eastward progression of the trough axis,
promoting clearing from west to east as a 1036 mb surface high
builds in from the Plains. The NBM has the area cooling 15 to 20 
degrees from Friday to Saturday, with eastern Kentucky remaining 
under continuous northerly cold air advection (CAA). Highs in the 
mid to upper 50s on Saturday will run 10 to 15 degrees below 
climatological normals. If guidance holds, clearing Saturday night
under these pattern dynamics will allow low temperatures to 
tumble into the upper 20s to lower 30s, effectively ending the 
growing season, at least in the sheltered valleys. This will be 
monitored, and if guidance holds and confidence grows, frost or 
freeze products may be forthcoming at the end of the week.
